rv.q: The play’s flaws matter less than the fact that it heightens awareness about Tibet and forces us to re-examine the potential of non-violence.
This is an intermittently powerful piece of theatre, but there are stretches where not everything convinces and when the dialogue descends into ideological sparring.

'Pah-La' is a very ambitious piece of work that attempts (among other things) to explain the relationship between China and Tibet, the nature of violence, language and anger, and their relation to Buddhism and also the patriarchy.
While it intrigues and sometimes startles, the play is frustratingly slippery and, for all its underlying complexity, strangely slender.

But even as it valuably and – given the climate – provocatively probes the nature of individual and collective resistance – and the relation between violent and non-violent protest – it heads into overly abstruse terrain.
It is an important, educational play, though the essence of it occupies a philosophical space somewhat above the plot, at times alienating its audience.

Yet Pah-La also has a curiously hazy and disjointed feel, with long speeches repeatedly reinforcing the same points, rather than developing the narrative or refining the relationships between the characters.

cn.t: Majumdar's extensively researched drama about Tibet's 2008 unrest offers a thoughtful philosophical inquiry into non-violence and oppression, though critics find the execution uneven and the technique flawed.
